summary.text: The nervous system is the part of an animal that coordinates its actions and sensory information by sending signals to and from different parts of its body.
It detects changes in the environment that affect the body, then works together with the endocrine system to respond to them.
In vertebrates it has two main parts: the central nervous system, made of the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system, made mainly of nerves.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: Arose in wormlike organisms about 550 to 600 million years ago

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: Few hundred cells in simplest worms; 300 billion in elephants

facts.label: Who studies it
facts.value: Neuroscience studies it; neurology studies its disorders

items.prompt: A person sits calmly on a couch, fully relaxed. Which part of the autonomic nervous system is mostly active?
items.explain: The parasympathetic system is the one activated when an organism is in a relaxed state, while the sympathetic system handles emergencies.

items.prompt: A driver slams the brakes to avoid a crash and feels a surge of energy. Which system just switched on to mobilize it?
items.explain: The sympathetic nervous system is activated in emergencies to mobilize energy.

items.prompt: You touch a hot mug and information races from your hand toward your central nervous system. Which nerves carry it?
items.explain: Nerves carrying information from the body to the CNS are sensory (afferent) nerves; motor nerves carry signals away from the brain.

items.prompt: A biologist compares a jellyfish with a cat. How does the jellyfish's nervous system differ in layout?

options.label: It is a brain with one cord and nerves branching off
It has no nervous system because it is so simple
It is a single thick nerve running through the body
It is a diffuse nerve net of loosely connected cells

items.explain: Jellyfish are radially symmetric, and their nervous system is a diffuse nerve net. Most other animals have a brain, a central cord and nerves radiating from them.

items.prompt: Neurons do the signalling, but other cells give them structural and metabolic support. What are those helper cells called?
items.explain: Glial cells, or glia, are the non-neuronal cells that support neurons structurally and metabolically.

items.prompt: A surgeon says an injury affects the central nervous system. Which pair of structures is the central nervous system made of?

options.label: The brain and the spinal cord

items.explain: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord, while the nerves belong to the peripheral nervous system.

choices.label: The parasympathetic nervous system
choices.feedback: It sounds like the body's alarm, but it is the branch active when an organism is relaxed.

choices.label: The enteric nervous system
choices.feedback: It is part of the autonomic system, but its job is to control the gastrointestinal system.

right.label: Carry information from the body to the CNS

beats.explain: Nerves are named either for the direction their signals travel or for where they leave the central nervous system.

beats.prompt: sort each into its part of the vertebrate nervous system
beats.explain: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the PNS is mainly the nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about a jellyfish is wrong; which?

steps.text: The nervous system coordinates an animal by sending signals.
A jellyfish is an animal, so it has a nervous system.
Its nervous system, like ours, is built around a brain and a central cord.
So its signals travel through nervous tissue.

beats.explain: Jellyfish nervous systems are a diffuse nerve net. A brain with a central cord is the pattern for most other animals.

beats.idea: The nervous system sends signals along nerves to and from a central hub, with one branch ready for emergencies and another for rest.

paragraphs.heading: The body's signalling network
paragraphs.text: The nervous system is the part of an animal that coordinates what it does and what it senses, by passing signals between different parts of its body. It picks up changes in the surroundings that affect the body. Then it works together with the endocrine system to respond to them.

paragraphs.heading: Central and peripheral
paragraphs.text: In vertebrates it has two main parts. The central nervous system, or CNS, is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system, or PNS, is made mostly of nerves: wrapped bundles of long fibres called axons that link the CNS to every other part of the body. Nerves carrying signals out from the brain are motor nerves, and nerves carrying information from the body to the CNS are sensory nerves.

paragraphs.heading: Automatic branches
paragraphs.text: The PNS splits into the somatic and the autonomic nervous systems. The autonomic part divides again into three. The sympathetic system switches on in emergencies to mobilise energy, the parasympathetic system works when the animal is relaxed, and the enteric system runs the gut.

paragraphs.heading: Neurons and glia
paragraphs.text: Nervous tissue is defined by a special cell, the neuron. Neurons send fast, precise signals as electrochemical impulses along their axons. At a junction called a synapse, the signal either passes straight across electrically or makes the neuron release chemicals called neurotransmitters. Alongside neurons are glial cells, or glia, which give structural and metabolic support; in the human brain there are roughly as many glia as neurons.

paragraphs.heading: From signals to behaviour
paragraphs.text: A cell that gets a signal from a neuron can be excited, inhibited or changed in some other way. Linked neurons form pathways, circuits and bigger networks. These networks produce an animal's perception of the world and decide how it behaves.

paragraphs.heading: Across the animal kingdom
paragraphs.text: Most many-celled animals have a nervous system, but they range widely in complexity. Sponges, placozoans and mesozoans have none at all. Jellyfish, corals and their relatives have a diffuse nerve net. In the simplest worms the whole system has only a few hundred cells, while an African elephant's has around 300 billion.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: The nervous system can fail through genetic defects, injury, poisons, infection or simply ageing. Neurology is the branch of medicine that studies these disorders and looks for ways to prevent or treat them. In the PNS the most common problem is nerves failing to conduct signals, as in diabetic neuropathy or multiple sclerosis.
